title: Contracting triangular cell for mixed-commuting rank-one generators
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Groups are affine $F$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Write $\mathbf G_a,\mathbf G_m$ for [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth and connected and $T\subseteq G$ a split maximal torus, that is, a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ and maximal among such subgroups. Write $N_G(T)$ for the subgroup functor normalizing $T$ after every scalar extension. Put $X=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf G_m,T)$, paired by $\chi\circ\eta(t)=t^{\langle\chi,\eta\rangle}$. Let $D\subset X\setminus\{0\}$ be finite, nonempty and $\mathbf Z$-linearly independent. For each $\alpha\in D$ let $J_\alpha\subseteq G$ be split reductive with maximal torus $T$ and roots exactly $\pm\alpha$, with conventions as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Denote its root groups by $U_\alpha,V_\alpha=U_{-\alpha}$ [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. Assume $G$ is the smallest closed subgroup containing these $J_\alpha$, and that $V_\alpha$ commutes scheme-theoretically with $U_\beta$ whenever $\alpha\ne\beta$. Let $U,V$ be the smallest closed subgroups containing the $U_\alpha$, respectively the $V_\alpha$. For a cocharacter $\eta$, let $U_G(\eta)$ be the subgroup functor of points $g$ for which $\eta(t)g\eta(t)^{-1}$ extends to $t=0$ with value $1$, and let $Z_G(\eta)$ be the subgroup functor centralizing $\eta(\mathbf G_m)$ after every scalar extension. Choose $\lambda\in Y$ and $n>0$ with $\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle=n$ for every $\alpha\in D$. Then $U,V$ are smooth connected unipotent subgroups normalized by $T$, the products $TU$ and $TV$ are smooth connected solvable closed subgroups, and multiplication $V\times_F T\times_F U\to G$ is an open immersion with dense image. One has $U=U_G(\lambda)$, $V=U_G(-\lambda)$, $Z_G(\lambda)=T$ and $(TU)\cap(TV)=T$ as subgroup schemes. Solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic derived subgroups terminate at the identity. Unipotent means that geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. No reductivity hypothesis is imposed on $G$.

source.place: Theorem 23.31, printed p.494; the triangular-cell argument 23.22, pp.491--492, and cocharacter limit groups Theorem 13.33, pp.265--266. Supporting assertion: contracting positive/negative generated groups and their open cell (Steinberg 1999, 5.6--5.10).

proof.text: Put $U_+=U_G(\lambda)$, $U_-=U_G(-\lambda)$, $Z=Z_G(\lambda)$, and let $P_\pm$ be the corresponding limit-exists groups. The cocharacter structure lemma makes these smooth connected closed subgroups, with $U_\pm$ unipotent and $P_+=U_+\rtimes Z$. To check intersections without losing infinitesimal points, take a faithful closed embedding of $G$ from the faithful-weight-block lemma with central torus $1$, and a weight basis for $\lambda$ with weights $m_1\ge\cdots\ge m_N$. On every test algebra conjugation multiplies entry $g_{ij}$ by $t^{m_i-m_j}$. Thus $P_+$ is block upper triangular, $P_-$ block lower triangular, $Z$ block diagonal, and $U_\pm$ have identity diagonal blocks. In particular $P_+\cap P_-=Z$ and $U_-\cap P_+=1$ as functors. The Lie-weight formulas give $\operatorname{Lie}(U_-)\oplus\operatorname{Lie}(P_+)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. The transverse-product theorem therefore makes multiplication $U_-\times P_+\to G$ an open immersion. Reordering $U_+\rtimes Z$ gives an open immersion $U_-\times Z\times U_+\to G$; denote its image by $\Omega$.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(a)--(e), pp.265--266; matrix proof and transverse multiplication.

proof.text: For every $\alpha$, the root parametrization gives $\lambda(t)u_\alpha(a)\lambda(t)^{-1}=u_\alpha(t^n a)$; the negative-root formula has exponent $-n$. Consequently $U_\alpha\subset U_+$ and $V_\alpha\subset U_-$, and minimality gives $U\subset U_+$, $V\subset U_-$. Here the inclusions hold on all test algebras. For smoothness and connectedness of $U$, enumerate $D=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d\}$ and use the multiplication map from the palindromic product $X=U_{\alpha_1}\times\cdots\times U_{\alpha_d}\times U_{\alpha_d}\times\cdots\times U_{\alpha_1}$ to $G$, pointed at the identities. Its image is inverse-stable on every algebra, and each root group occurs by setting other coordinates to the identity. Its coordinate ring over any field extension is a polynomial ring, hence a domain; thus $X$ is geometrically reduced and connected. The pointed-map generation lemma identifies its generated group with $U$ and makes $U$ geometrically reduced and connected. The geometrically-reduced group lemma makes it smooth. Repeat with the $V_\alpha$ to obtain the same conclusions for $V$. Both are unipotent by restriction of the faithful representations of $U_+$ and $U_-$.

source.place: Section 2h, Propositions 2.46--2.48, pp.54--55; root conjugation formula (135), p.431; cocharacter kernels, pp.265--266.

proof.text: The same coordinate construction records the density needed below. For $U$ its defining ideal is $I=\bigcap_{q\ge1}\ker(F[G]\to F[X^q])$. Since each $X^q$ is an affine space, the Nullstellensatz vanishing principle shows that a function vanishing on all rational root words belongs to $I$. Hence those words are schematically dense in $U$; likewise the negative words are schematically dense in $V$. For each $J_\alpha$, the rank-one reflection lemma gives $\operatorname{Lie}(J_\alpha)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\mathfrak j_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak j_{-\alpha}$, the last two summands being the tangent lines of its root groups. The smooth-subgroup tangent-generation lemma shows that $T,U_\alpha,V_\alpha$ generate $J_\alpha$. Thus $T$ and all signed root groups generate $G$. Apply the pointed-map construction to a palindromic product containing $T$ and all signed root groups. Its source and all powers have Laurent polynomial coordinate domains, and its image is inverse-stable. Minimality identifies the resulting group with $G$; the same ideal calculation and vanishing principle show that the abstract subgroup $\Gamma\subset G(F)$ generated by these rational points is schematically dense in $G$.

source.place: Section 2h, pp.54--56; Theorem 21.11(b),(c),(f), pp.428--430; generated-group density as used in 23.22.

proof.text: The root conjugation formulas also show that $T$ normalizes $U$ and $V$ scheme-theoretically. Indeed conjugation acts on each palindromic parameter space and commutes with its word map; hence every word-map kernel is preserved by the torus coaction, and so is their intersection. This last assertion can be checked coefficient by coefficient in the Laurent monomial basis of $F[T]$. Also $T\subset Z$ since it is commutative. Define $C$ to be the reduced closed subscheme whose underlying set is the closure of $V(F)T(F)U(F)$ in $G$. Left translation by $V(F)$ and by $T(F)$ preserves this closure: $V$ is a group and $T$ normalizes both factors. We shall prove $C=G$. This is a density argument only; at this point no reductivity of $G$ or openness of the smaller product has been used.

source.place: The setup and closure argument of 23.21--23.22, p.491; torus normalization checked on the universal word maps.

proof.text:
Choose for each $J_\alpha$ the opposite-root $\operatorname{SL}_2$ homomorphism, and use its upper and lower parameters for $u_\alpha,v_\alpha$. In $\operatorname{SL}_2$, direct multiplication, with $d=1+ab$ invertible, gives
$$x_+(a)x_-(b)=x_-(b/d)h(d)x_+(a/d).$$
Indeed both matrices have entries $(1+ab,a,b,1)$ in row order: the lower-right entry on the right is $(ab+1)/d=1$. Applying the homomorphism gives the same identity in $J_\alpha$, with $h(d)$ replaced by $\alpha^\vee(d)\in T$. This is valid in every characteristic and for all test algebras with $d$ invertible. It requires no arbitrary reparametrization of a root group and no assertion that this formula holds when $d=0$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11 proof and opposite-root parametrizations, pp.429--430; explicit Gauss identity supplying the rank-one replacement in 23.22.

proof.text: We prove by induction on $q$ that $u_\alpha(a)v_{\beta_1}(b_1)\cdots v_{\beta_q}(b_q)$ lies in $C(F)$ for every rational tuple and every choice of indices. For $q=0$ it belongs to $U(F)$. If $\alpha\ne\beta_1$, mixed commutation moves $v_{\beta_1}(b_1)$ to the left; the induction hypothesis and left $V(F)$-stability of $C$ apply. If $\alpha=\beta_1$, first work on the principal open $1+ab_1\ne0$ of the affine parameter space. Step 5 writes the product as $v_\alpha(b_1/d)\alpha^\vee(d)$ times a word beginning with $u_\alpha(a/d)$ followed by $q-1$ negative factors. The latter belongs to $C(F)$ by induction; left $V(F)$- and $T(F)$-stability give the assertion there. To include the exceptional locus, pull back any equation of $C$ along the original polynomial word map. It vanishes at all rational points of this principal open, so vanishes in its reduced localization by the Nullstellensatz. Since $1+ab_1$ is a nonzero polynomial in a polynomial domain, the localization is injective, so it vanishes everywhere. This completes the induction, including $d=0$.

source.place: 23.22, p.491, induction (149); explicit localization argument replaces an unjustified use of Gauss decomposition on the exceptional locus.

proof.text: Fix $u=u_\alpha(a)\in U_\alpha(F)$. For each defining equation $f$ of $C$, the function $v\mapsto f(uv)$ on $V$ vanishes on every negative root word by step 6. The schematic density from step 3 implies that it is zero. Thus $uV(F)\subset C(F)$. Right translation by $U(F)$ and $T(F)$ preserves $C$: it preserves $V(F)T(F)U(F)$ because $U$ is a group normalized by $T$. Hence $uvtu\prime\in C(F)$ for every $v\in V(F)$, $t\in T(F)$ and $u\prime\in U(F)$. Therefore $u$ preserves the closure $C$ under left translation. Both $u$ and $u^{-1}$ have this property. Together with left $V(F)$- and $T(F)$-stability, every element of $\Gamma$ preserves $C$. Since $1\in C$, $\Gamma\subset C(F)$. By its schematic density in $G$, every equation of $C$ is zero. Hence $C=G$ and $V(F)T(F)U(F)$ is dense in $G$.

source.place: 23.22, p.491, passage from (149) to stability under the generating groups; density is the explicit coordinate-ideal consequence established in step 3.

proof.text: In the open chart $\Omega\simeq U_-\times Z\times U_+$ of step 1, the morphism $V\times T\times U\to\Omega$ is the product of three closed immersions, since $V\subset U_-$, $T\subset Z$ and $U\subset U_+$. It is therefore a closed immersion in this chart. Its image contains the dense subset $V(F)T(F)U(F)$ of $G$, so its underlying closed subset is all of $\Omega$. Moreover $\Omega$ is reduced: the smoothness of $G$ implies geometric reducedness. A defining ideal whose vanishing locus is all of a reduced affine scheme is zero, since each of its elements is nilpotent. Apply this on affine opens of $\Omega$. Thus $V\times T\times U\xrightarrow{\sim}\Omega$. Pulling this equality back along each coordinate axis gives $V=U_-$, $T=Z$, $U=U_+$ as closed subschemes. Multiplication is consequently the asserted open immersion with dense image. This upgrades the rational-point density argument to all test algebras, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(d), pp.265--266, together with 23.22--23.23, pp.491--492; closed subproduct inside the universal cocharacter chart.

proof.text: Since $Z=T$, the cocharacter semidirect-product isomorphisms identify $TU=P_+$ and $TV=P_-$ as closed subgroup schemes. Both are smooth and connected, and step 1 gives $(TU)\cap(TV)=P_+\cap P_-=Z=T$ on every test algebra. Their projections to $T$ have kernels $U,V$. These kernels are smooth unipotent and hence solvable by the unipotent-solvability lemma. Its finite normal series with commutative quotients forces termination of successive derived subgroups: if $U=U_0\supset\cdots\supset U_l=1$ is such a series, commutators in $U_i$ lie in $U_{i+1}$, so $\mathcal D^iU\subset U_i$. For $P_+$ the commutative torus quotient forces $\mathcal D P_+\subset U$, and then $\mathcal D^{l+1}P_+=1$. The argument for $P_-$ is identical. Thus solvability has exactly the scheme-theoretic derived-series meaning in the item.

source.place: Theorem 13.33(b),(e), pp.265--266; unipotent solvability, Proposition 14.21, pp.284--285.

proof_origin.place: 23.22, p.491, word-length induction; Theorem 13.33, pp.265--266, supplies the ambient cocharacter chart. Universal-coordinate details and the closed-subproduct argument are supplied explicitly.
